the opposing side's counsel argued the executive's recognition power is exclusive under the Constitution.
Justices questioned whether the side that brought the case's view limits the President's future flexibility.

case.dek: A citizen wants the State Department to list Israel as his birthplace. The President refuses, claiming exclusive control over foreign recognition.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the balance of power between Congress and the President on foreign policy. the side that brought the case argues Congress can mandate passport entries. the opposing side argues the President alone controls recognition.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 24, lines 5-25

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on November 7, 2011.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 3, lines 7-17

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the court to order the State Department to list Israel as the birthplace on his passport.
the opposing side wants the court to uphold the President's refusal to list Israel as the birthplace.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 24, lines 5-25

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues Congress holds shared power over foreign relations and can override executive judgment.
the opposing side argues the President holds exclusive constitutional power to recognize foreign states.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 24, lines 5-25

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Kennedy asked if any foreign relations determinations remain exclusively for the President under the side that brought the case's theory.
Justice Ginsburg asked why Congress trumps the executive if foreign relations is a shared power.
